nameStory: Pleurotaenium coronatum gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'side ribbon' and 'crowned,' referring to its elongated, ribbon-like shape and the distinctive crown-like ornamentations at its ends. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, microscopists sometimes call members of this group 'desmids' or simply refer to them by their scientific names.
description: Pleurotaenium coronatum is a microscopic single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater environments. This tiny organism has an elegant, elongated cylindrical shape that looks like a delicate glass rod or narrow tube under magnification. Individual cells are typically 10-20 times longer than they are wide, reaching lengths of about 200-400 micrometers (roughly the width of a few human hairs). You'll need a microscope to see these beautiful creatures, as they're invisible to the naked eye.

idTips.label: Elongated cylindrical shape
idTips.description: Under a microscope, appears as a long, narrow cylinder or rod-like structure, much longer than it is wide, with relatively straight sides

idTips.label: Crowned ends
idTips.description: Each end of the cell features distinctive ornamental structures that look like tiny crowns or decorative caps when viewed under high magnification

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Appears bright green under the microscope due to chloroplasts (the parts that do photosynthesis) distributed throughout the cell

idTips.label: Single-celled structure
idTips.description: Each individual is a complete single cell with no division into separate compartments or segments along its length

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The outer surface appears smooth and glassy under magnification, without obvious bumps, ridges, or textured patterns

habitat: Found in clean, acidic freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in bog pools, pristine ponds, and slow-moving streams with soft water. These microscopic algae prefer nutrient-poor waters and are often indicators of good water quality. You're most likely to find them in undisturbed wetlands, especially in areas with sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water temperatures warm and daylight hours lengthen, making this a good time to find them in pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when growth conditions are optimal and populations are most easily found in water samples.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though they can still be found with careful sampling.
seasonality.winter: Present in low numbers under ice cover, entering a dormant phase but remaining viable until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Pleurotaenium coronatum is actually a sophisticated single cell that can be longer than some small insects - imagine a cell so elongated it's like a microscopic green needle floating in pond water!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other elongated desmid algae like Closterium species, but Pleurotaenium has straighter sides and distinctive crown-like end ornaments, while Closterium species are typically crescent-shaped or curved. Remember: Pleurotaenium = straight with crowns, Closterium = curved like a crescent moon.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'desmid' comes from Greek meaning 'chain' or 'bond,' though many desmids like Pleurotaenium actually live as individual cells rather than in chains. These algae are considered living jewels of the microscopic world and are prized by microscopists for their geometric beauty and precision.
compareHints: Pleurotaenium coronatum differs from its relatives by having the most pronounced crown-like ornaments at the cell ends - P. ehrenbergii and P. trabecula have simpler, less ornate end structures. P. maximum is significantly larger, while P. nodosum has distinctive swollen areas along the cell body that coronatum lacks.
